clue.text: Attendants dig Italian wines out

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or put out of place, so the letters leave their order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Waiters are told to go and fetch the Italian wines from the cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spells LADIES-IN-WAITING across 1 and 10; the three fodder words together supply exactly its fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladies-in-waiting are women who serve a queen or princess, so they are royal attendants.

clue.text: Spooner’s Lady Fortune for company in trouble

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of neighbouring words

blocks.note: a dame is a titled lady; it takes the L from the other word
luck is fortune; it takes the D from the other word

explanation.surface: Someone prays to Lady Luck for help with a firm that is struggling.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Fortune becomes DAME LUCK; swapping the D and L gives LAME DUCK.
explanation.definitionFit: In business slang a lame duck is a failing firm that needs rescue or support to survive.

clue.text: Operas at Bayreuth occasion bold action

blocks.note: Der Ring des Nibelungen, Wagner's opera cycle staged at Bayreuth
a do is a party or social occasion

explanation.surface: A night of Wagner at the Bayreuth festival is treated as a daring event.
explanation.walkthrough: Wagner's Ring cycle is four operas, so 'Der Ring' fairly stands for plural operas; Bayreuth is the German town built around his festival.
explanation.definitionFit: Derring-do is heroic, daring behaviour, an old-fashioned term for brave deeds.

clue.text: Prince Henry in river having to breathe out

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits within the outer word

blocks.note: Hal is Shakespeare's name for young Prince Henry, later Henry V
the Exe is a river in Devon, England

explanation.surface: A prince falls into a river and needs to get his breath back.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Prince Hal is a crossword staple, and the Exe, a river in Devon, turns up constantly as a three-letter river.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhaling is the act of expelling air from the lungs, the plain synonym of breathing out.

clue.text: Rest ordered to protect long sewer

indicators.note: putting things in order means rearranging them into a new sequence
protecting something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A doctor orders bed rest to guard a lengthy drainage pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewer' reads as a drain pronounced SOO-er, but it is someone who sews, pronounced SO-er.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sews works with needle and thread, making stitches, so a sewer is a stitcher.

clue.text: Wooden floor collapsed in Tennessee building

indicators.note: something collapsed has fallen apart, so its letters end up in a jumble
placing one thing in another puts it inside the outer word

blocks.note: TN is the US postal abbreviation for Tennessee
eleven letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wooden floor has given way in some building in Tennessee.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged floor letters go between T and N.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tower of London is a historic castle and fortress on the Thames, a famous building.

clue.text: Capital made by Republican taking hint about oil supply

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece goes round another
'supply' read as supple-ly means flexibly, so these letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: a tip is a hint
standard abbreviation for Republican
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A politician wins power in a capital city by controlling the oil supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a noun but is the adverb from supple, meaning flexibly.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the capital city of Libya, a country whose economy rests on oil exports.

clue.text: One in crowd offers lift

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a host is a great crowd, as in a host of angels

explanation.surface: Someone in a crowd offers a person a lift home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lift' looks like a ride in a car; here it is the verb to raise.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoist something is to raise it, often with ropes or tackle, so it matches lift as a verb.

clue.text: View communist eating fish

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: red is the colour of communism
the gar is a long-snouted freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A description of a communist eating fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'View' looks like a noun opening a scene; it is the verb to look at. The fish is a favourite short one in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To regard something is to look at or consider it, a synonym of view as a verb.

clue.text: Month in advance

blocks.note: first meaning: the third month of the year
second meaning: to move forward steadily, as troops do

explanation.walkthrough: 'in advance' reads as beforehand, but 'in' only joins two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the third calendar month and also the verb for troops walking forward in step.

clue.text: See 1
Pigheadedness a sign in recent changes

indicators.note: things that change take a new form, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: thirteen letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Stubbornness is taken as a signal behind some recent policy shifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' looks like a noun in the surface; it is the verb telling you to rearrange the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Intransigence is a refusal to compromise or alter one's views, which is stubbornness.

clue.text: Little water fowl back to meet obstruction

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: a fowl is a bird
a let is an old word for a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A small waterbird turns back when it hits an obstacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little water fowl' looks like a duckling; the definition is only 'Little water'.
explanation.definitionFit: A driblet is a tiny quantity of liquid, a small drop or trickle.

clue.text: Chicken roll containing nothing

indicators.note: containing means holding within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a roll is a list of names, a roster
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A bread roll with no filling at all, or a chicken sandwich without chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roll' suggests bread but is a register of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male domestic fowl, the cockerel, so it is a kind of chicken.

clue.text: Composer’s pen

blocks.note: first meaning: an American avant-garde composer famous for a silent piece
second meaning: an enclosure for animals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer's pen' suggests the thing he writes with; the 's is 'is', joining a composer's name to an enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cage wrote the silent piece 4'33", and a cage, like a pen, is an enclosure that confines animals.

clue.text: In restaurant’s fine-ground stimulant

indicators.note: ground means crushed, like coffee beans, so the letters are broken up and remade
one thing being in another means it sits within the outer word

blocks.note: a café is a small restaurant
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A café's finely ground coffee is what gives customers their buzz.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the wordplay to the definition; 'ground' fits the coffee picture but signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Caffeine is the drug in coffee and tea that makes people alert, a classic stimulant.

clue.text: Scrambling device used in Yankee helicopter

blocks.note: first meaning: a kitchen whisk for scrambling eggs
second meaning: American slang for a chopper, from its whirling blades

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrambling device' suggests a code scrambler used by the military; it is the kitchen whisk. Yankee means American here.
explanation.definitionFit: The whisk beats eggs, and Americans nickname a helicopter after it because its rotor spins the same way.

clue.text: Might we soon need this one as pot boils?

definitions.text: Might we soon need this one as pot boils?

indicators.note: boiling water churns and bubbles, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: eight letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Waiting for the kettle, someone reaches for the thing needed to make tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while the last words also supply its letters, so it is an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: When the water boils for a cuppa you need a small spoon to add sugar or stir the brew.

clue.text: Old rhyme about house – one outside Oxford?

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for old
rhyme is verse
HO is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: An old nursery rhyme about a house somewhere near Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' reads as the city, but an Oxford is a laced shoe, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: An overshoe is a protective cover worn over ordinary footwear such as an Oxford brogue.

clue.text: Essence contained in letter backing Lackland’s one

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run in reverse
being contained in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: tee is the spelt-out name of the letter T
the pith of something is its essence or core

explanation.surface: A description of the essential spirit found in a letter backing King John.
explanation.walkthrough: King John of England was nicknamed Lackland because he inherited no lands; that nickname is his.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive nickname attached to a person, like Lackland for King John.

clue.text: Flesh-eating monster making some progress

indicators.note: 'some' of a word is only part of it, so the answer is a run of letters inside

blocks.note: found inside the letters of this word

explanation.surface: A man-eating monster is gaining ground on its victims.
explanation.walkthrough: The four letters run through the middle of 'progress'.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore an ogre is a giant that devours humans, a monster that eats flesh.

clue.text: Body Romeo dragged into thicket

indicators.note: dragging something into a place puts it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a copse is a small thicket of trees
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A body is found where Romeo was pulled into the bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is not Shakespeare's lover but the radio code word for R.
explanation.definitionFit: A corpse is a dead human body, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Rare fright catching cold

indicators.note: catching something means holding it, so one piece is caught inside another

blocks.note: a scare is a fright
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: An unusual scare in which someone comes down with a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' could be steak; here it simply means uncommon.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scarce is in short supply and seldom found, which is what rare means.

clue.text: Initial opportunity

blocks.note: first meaning: first, as in the first move of a game
second meaning: a chance or vacancy

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase, a first chance; they are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for the first in a sequence and a noun for a chance or job vacancy.

clue.text: One partial to fish, Ruth having no starter

indicators.note: with no starter the first course is skipped, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: ruth is an old word for sorrow or remorse

explanation.surface: Someone fond of fish, perhaps a diner named Ruth, skips the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth' looks like a name but is the old noun behind 'ruthless'.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a heron-like wading bird that feeds on fish, so it is fond of them.

clue.text: Returning hero knows Scots writer

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: El Cid is the Spanish national hero
in Scots, to ken is to know

explanation.surface: A war hero comes home and recognises a Scottish author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots' looks like it describes the writer; it flags that 'knows' is a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens is the English Victorian novelist of Oliver Twist, a famous writer.

clue.text: Dolly perhaps bringing female inside temple

indicators.note: inside means within, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: Dolly Parton is the American country singer; 'perhaps' shows she is one example
a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: Dolly brings a woman along to a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dolly' is not a doll but a surname clue: Parton, one of several famous people named Dolly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parthenon is the ancient temple of Athena on the Acropolis in Athens.

clue.text: Spanish banker clutching at relationship

indicators.note: clutching means gripping tightly, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: río is Spanish for river, and a river is a banker because it has banks
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spanish banker holds on to a business relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is crossword code for a river, something with banks; Spanish gives RIO.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio expresses the quantitative relationship between two amounts, such as three to one.

clue.text: Championship secured in final with style?

indicators.note: being secured in something means held within it

blocks.note: the final part is the end
a championship is a title

explanation.surface: A champion wins the title in the final with a stylish performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with style' suggests flair, but a style is a formal title, such as Sir or Lady; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone entitled holds a title, and a person's formal style is the form of address their rank gives them.

clue.text: Excitable thing in north going after new money

indicators.note: going after means following, so one piece is placed at the end

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for new
the euro is a currency
standard abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Someone in the north gets excited about coming into fresh cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excitable thing' sounds like a person; it is a nerve cell, which biologists call excitable because it fires signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Neurons are nerve cells that respond to stimuli by firing electrical impulses, which biologists call excitability.
